claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the neural encoding of attention direction.

claims.claim: The alpha power band could be tracked to determine the locus of auditory attention.
claims.source: A few studies employing MEG have suggested that in particular the alpha power band could be tracked to determine the locus of auditory attention (Frey et al., 2014; Wöstmann et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Frey et al., 2014 and Wöstmann et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The beta power band is related with selective attention.
claims.source: Another study, employing scalp EEG, found the beta power band related with selective attention (Gao et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gao et al., 2017.

claims.claim: EEG data was collected from 16 normal-hearing subjects while they listened to two competing speakers and were instructed to attend to one particular speaker.
claims.source: EEG data was collected from 16 normal-hearing subjects while they listened to two competing speakers and were instructed to attend to one particular speaker.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental setup used in the study.

claims.claim: The EEG data was recorded using a 64-channel BioSemi ActiveTwo system, at a sampling rate of 8196 Hz.
claims.source: The EEG data was recorded using a 64-channel BioSemi ActiveTwo system, at a sampling rate of 8196 Hz, in an electromagnetically shielded and soundproof room.
claims.evidence: This describes the data acquisition methodology.

claims.claim: The auditory stimuli were low-pass filtered with a cutoff frequency of 4 kHz and presented at 60 dBA through Etymotic ER3 insert earphones.
claims.source: The auditory stimuli were low-pass filtered with a cutoff frequency of 4 kHz and presented at 60 dBA through Etymotic ER3 insert earphones.
claims.evidence: This describes the stimulus presentation methodology.

claims.claim: The auditory stimuli were comprised of four Dutch stories, narrated by three male Flemish speakers.
claims.source: The auditory stimuli were comprised of four Dutch stories, narrated by three male Flemish speakers (DeBuren, 2007).
claims.evidence: This describes the stimuli used in the experiment.

claims.claim: Each story was 12 min long and split into two parts of 6 min each.
claims.source: Each story was 12 min long and split into two parts of 6 min each.
claims.evidence: This describes the structure of the experimental stimuli.

claims.claim: Silent segments longer than 500 ms were shortened to 500 ms.
claims.source: Silent segments longer than 500 ms were shortened to 500 ms.
claims.evidence: This describes preprocessing of the auditory stimuli.

claims.claim: The experiment was split into eight trials, each 6 min long.
claims.source: The experiment was split into eight trials, each 6 min long.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claims.claim: In every trial, subjects were presented with two parts of two different stories, one in the left ear and one in the right ear.
claims.source: In every trial, subjects were presented with two parts of two different stories. One part was presented in the left ear, while the other was presented in the right ear.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claims.claim: Subjects were instructed to attend to one of the two stories via a monitor positioned in front of them.
claims.source: Subjects were instructed to attend to one of the two via a monitor positioned in front of them.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claims.claim: After each trial, subjects completed a multiple-choice quiz about the attended story.
claims.source: After each trial, subjects completed a multiple-choice quiz about the attended story.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental procedure for assessing attention.

claims.claim: There was 8 × 6 min = 48 min of data per subject.
claims.source: In total, there was 8 × 6 min = 48 min of data per subject.
claims.evidence: This is a calculation based on the experimental design.

claims.claim: The EEG data was filtered with an equiripple FIR bandpass filter and its group delay was compensated for.
claims.source: The EEG data was filtered with an equiripple FIR bandpass filter and its group delay was compensated for.
claims.evidence: This describes the data preprocessing methodology.

claims.claim: For use with linear models, the EEG was filtered between 1 and 9 Hz, which has been found to be an optimal frequency range for linear attention decoding.
claims.source: For use with linear models, the EEG was filtered between 1 and 9 Hz, which has been found to be an optimal frequency range for linear attention decoding (Pasley et al., 2012; Ding and Simon, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pasley et al., 2012 and Ding and Simon, 2012.

claims.claim: For the CNN models, a broader bandwidth between 1 and 32 Hz was used, as this is more optimal.
claims.source: For the CNN models, a broader bandwidth between 1 and 32 Hz was used, as Taillez et al., 2017 show that this is more optimal.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Taillez et al., 2017.

claims.claim: After the bandpass filtering, the EEG data was downsampled to 20 Hz for the linear model and 128 Hz for the CNN.
claims.source: After the bandpass filtering, the EEG data was downsampled to 20 Hz (linear model) and 128 Hz (CNN).
claims.evidence: This describes the data preprocessing methodology.

claims.claim: Artifacts were removed with the generic MWF-based removal algorithm described in Somers et al., 2018.
claims.source: Artifacts were removed with the generic MWF-based removal algorithm described in Somers et al., 2018.
claims.evidence: This describes the artifact removal methodology with a citation.

claims.claim: Data of each subject was divided into a training, validation, and test set.
claims.source: Data of each subject was divided into a training, validation, and test set.
claims.evidence: This describes the data partitioning methodology.

claims.claim: Data segments were generated with a sliding window equal in size to the chosen window length and with an overlap of 50%.
claims.source: Per set, data segments were generated with a sliding window equal in size to the chosen window length and with an overlap of 50%.
claims.evidence: This describes the data segmentation methodology.

claims.claim: Data was normalized on a subject-by-subject basis, based on statistics of the training set only.
claims.source: Data was normalized on a subject-by-subject basis, based on statistics of the training set only, and in such a way that proportions between EEG channels were maintained.
claims.evidence: This describes the data normalization methodology.

claims.claim: The proposed CNN input is a 64 × T matrix, where 64 is the number of EEG channels and T is the number of samples in the decision window.
claims.source: The input is a 64 × T matrix, where 64 is the number of EEG channels in our dataset and T is the number of samples in the decision window.
claims.evidence: This describes the CNN architecture.

claims.claim: The first step in the CNN model is a convolutional layer with five independent 64 × 17 spatio-temporal filters.
claims.source: The first step in the model is a convolutional layer, indicated in blue. Five independent 64 × 17 spatio-temporal filters are shifted over the input matrix, which, since the first dimension is equal to the number of channels, each result in a time series of dimensions 1 × T.
claims.evidence: This describes the CNN architecture.

claims.claim: 130 ms was found to be an optimal filter width for the CNN.
claims.source: Note that '17' is 130 ms at 128 Hz, and 130 ms was found to be an optimal filter width – that is, longer or shorter decision window lengths gave a higher loss on a validation set.
claims.evidence: This is based on validation set performance.

claims.claim: A rectifying linear unit (ReLu) activation function is used after the convolution step in the CNN.
claims.source: A rectifying linear unit (ReLu) activation function is used after the convolution step.
claims.evidence: This describes the CNN architecture.

claims.claim: In the average pooling step, data is averaged over the time dimension, reducing each time series to a single number.
claims.source: In the average pooling step, data is averaged over the time dimension, thus reducing each time series to a single number.
claims.evidence: This describes the CNN architecture.

claims.claim: After the pooling step, there are two fully connected (FC) layers in the CNN.
claims.source: After the pooling step, there are two fully connected (FC) layers.
claims.evidence: This describes the CNN architecture.

claims.claim: The first fully connected layer contains five neurons and is followed by a sigmoid activation function.
claims.source: The first layer contains five neurons (one for each time series) and is followed by a sigmoid activation function, and the second layer contains two (output) neurons.
claims.evidence: This describes the CNN architecture.

claims.claim: The second fully connected layer contains two output neurons.
claims.source: The first layer contains five neurons (one for each time series) and is followed by a sigmoid activation function, and the second layer contains two (output) neurons.
claims.evidence: This describes the CNN architecture.

claims.claim: The two output neurons are connected to a cross-entropy loss function.
claims.source: These two neurons are connected to a cross-entropy loss function.
claims.evidence: This describes the CNN architecture.

claims.claim: The full CNN consists of approximately 5500 parameters.
claims.source: The full CNN consists of approximately 5500 parameters.
claims.evidence: This describes the CNN architecture.

claims.claim: The implementation was done in MATLAB 2016b and MatConvNet (version 1.0-beta25).
claims.source: The implementation was done in MATLAB 2016b and MatConvNet (version 1.0-beta25), a CNN toolbox for MATLAB (Vedaldi and Lenc, 2015).
claims.evidence: This describes the implementation details.

claims.claim: The model was trained on data of all subjects, including the subject it was tested on (but without using the same data for both training and testing).
claims.source: The model was trained on data of all subjects, including the subject it was tested on (but without using the same data for both training and testing).
claims.evidence: This describes the training methodology.

claims.claim: The data of the other subjects can be viewed as a regularization or data augmentation technique to avoid overfitting.
claims.source: This means we are training a subject-specific decoder, where the data of the other subjects can be viewed as a regularization or data augmentation technique to avoid overfitting on the (limited) amount of training data of the subject under test.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the training methodology.

claims.claim: The model was cross-validated over the four stories (resulting in four folds).
claims.source: To prevent the model from overfitting to one particular story, we cross-validated over the four stories (resulting in four folds).
claims.evidence: This describes the cross-validation methodology.

claims.claim: Only two folds were retained where the same speaker was never simultaneously part of both the training and the test set.
claims.source: Therefore, it is possible that the model gains an advantage by having 'seen' the EEG response to a specific speaker, so we retained only the folds wherein the same speaker was never simultaneously part of both the training and the test set. In the end, only two folds remained (see Table 2).
claims.evidence: This describes the cross-validation methodology.

claims.claim: The combined cross-validation approach is referred to as leave-one-story+speaker-out.
claims.source: We refer to the combined cross-validation approach as leave-one-story+speaker-out.
claims.evidence: This defines the terminology used in the study.

claims.claim: The network was trained by minimizing the cross-entropy between the network outputs and the corresponding labels.
claims.source: We trained the network by minimizing the cross-entropy between the network outputs and the corresponding labels (the attended ear).
claims.evidence: This describes the training methodology.

claims.claim: Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent was used with an initial learning rate of 0.09 and a momentum of 0.9.
claims.source: We used mini-batch stochastic gradient descent with an initial learning rate of 0.09 and a momentum of 0.9.
claims.evidence: This describes the training methodology.

claims.claim: A step decay learning schedule was applied that decreased the learning rate after epoch 10 and 35 to 0.045 and 0.0225, respectively.
claims.source: We applied a step decay learning schedule that decreased the learning rate after epoch 10 and 35 to 0.045 and 0.0225, respectively, to assure convergence.
claims.evidence: This describes the training methodology.

claims.claim: The batch size was set to 20.
claims.source: The batch size was set to 20, partly because of memory constraints, and partly because we did not see much improvement with larger batch sizes.
claims.evidence: This describes the training methodology.

claims.claim: Weights and biases were initialized by drawing randomly from a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 0.5.
claims.source: Weights and biases were initialized by drawing randomly from a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 0.5.
claims.evidence: This describes the training methodology.

claims.claim: Training ran for 100 epochs.
claims.source: Training ran for 100 epochs, as early experiments showed that the optimal decoder was usually found between epoch 70 and 95.
claims.evidence: This describes the training methodology.

claims.claim: Regularization consisted of weight decay with a value of 5 × 10–4.
claims.source: Regularization consisted of weight decay with a value of 5 × 10–4, and, after training, of selecting the decoder in the iteration where the validation loss was minimal.
claims.evidence: This describes the training methodology.

claims.claim: All hyperparameters were determined by running a grid search over a set of reasonable values.
claims.source: All hyperparameters given above were determined by running a grid search over a set of reasonable values.
claims.evidence: This describes the hyperparameter optimization methodology.

claims.claim: The decoding accuracy is defined as the percentage of correctly classified decision windows on the test set, averaged over the two folds.
claims.source: Note that in this work the decoding accuracy is defined as the percentage of correctly classified decision windows on the test set, averaged over the two folds mentioned earlier (one for each story narrated by a different speaker).
claims.evidence: This defines the performance metric used in the study.

claims.claim: A linear stimulus reconstruction model was used as baseline.
claims.source: A linear stimulus reconstruction model (Biesmans et al., 2017) was used as baseline.
claims.evidence: This describes the baseline model with a citation.

claims.claim: In the linear model, a spatio-temporal filter was trained and applied on the EEG data and its time-shifted versions up to 250 ms delay, based on least-squares regression.
claims.source: In this model, a spatio-temporal filter was trained and applied on the EEG data and its time-shifted versions up to 250 ms delay, based on least-squares regression, in order to reconstruct the envelope of the attended stimulus.
claims.evidence: This describes the baseline model methodology.

claims.claim: The envelopes were calculated with the 'powerlaw subbands' method proposed by Biesmans et al., 2017.
claims.source: The envelopes were calculated with the 'powerlaw subbands' method proposed by Biesmans et al., 2017; that is, a gammatone filter bank was used to split the speech into subbands, and per subband the envelope was calculated with a power law compression with exponent 0.6.
claims.evidence: This describes the envelope extraction methodology with a citation.

claims.claim: The linear model was also trained in a leave-one-story+speaker-out way.
claims.source: For a fairer comparison with the CNN, the linear model was also trained in a leave-one-story+speaker-out way.
claims.evidence: This describes the training methodology for the baseline model.

claims.claim: The linear model was not trained on any other data than that of the subject under testing.
claims.source: In contrast to the CNN, however, the linear model was not trained on any other data than that of the subject under testing, since including data of other subjects harms the performance of the linear model.
claims.evidence: This describes the training methodology for the baseline model.

claims.claim: The linear model is only able to relate the EEG to the envelopes of the recorded audio, while the CNN is free to extract any feature it finds optimal from the EEG.
claims.source: Note that the results of the linear model here merely serve as a representative baseline, and that a comparison between the two models should be treated with care – in part because the CNN is nonlinear, but also because the linear model is only able to relate the EEG to the envelopes of the recorded audio, while the CNN is free to extract any feature it finds optimal (though only from the EEG, as no audio is given to the CNN).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the differences between the two models.

claims.claim: Seven different decision window lengths were tested: 10, 5, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.25, and 0.13 s.
claims.source: Seven different decision window lengths were tested: 10, 5, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.25, and 0.13 s.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claims.claim: The reported accuracy for each subject is the mean accuracy of 10 different training runs of the model, each with a different (random) initialization.
claims.source: To capture the general performance of the CNN, the reported accuracy for each subject is the mean accuracy of 10 different training runs of the model, each with a different (random) initialization.
claims.evidence: This describes the evaluation methodology.

claims.claim: The linear model was not evaluated at a decision window length of 0.13 s since its kernel has a width of 0.25 s.
claims.source: The linear model was not evaluated at a decision window length of 0.13 s since its kernel has a width of 0.25 s, which places a lower bound on the possible decision window length.
claims.evidence: This describes a limitation of the baseline model.

claims.claim: For both decision windows (1 s and 10 s), the CNN had a higher median decoding accuracy than the linear model, but a larger intersubject variability.
claims.source: For both decision windows, the CNN had a higher median decoding accuracy, but a larger intersubject variability.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the results shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Two subjects had a decoding accuracy lower than 50% at a window length of 10 s and were not considered in the subsequent analysis.
claims.source: Two subjects had a decoding accuracy lower than 50% at a window length of 10 s, and were therefore not considered in the subsequent analysis, nor are they shown in the figures in this section.
claims.evidence: This describes the data exclusion criteria.

claims.claim: For 1 s decision windows, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test yielded significant differences in detection accuracy between the linear decoder model and the CNN (W = 3, p < 0.001).
claims.source: For 1 s decision windows, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test yielded significant differences in detection accuracy between the linear decoder model and the CNN (W = 3, p < 0.001), with an increase in median accuracy from 58.1 to 80.8%.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical test result based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: For 1 s decision windows, the median accuracy increased from 58.1% for the linear model to 80.8% for the CNN.
claims.source: For 1 s decision windows, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test yielded significant differences in detection accuracy between the linear decoder model and the CNN (W = 3, p < 0.001), with an increase in median accuracy from 58.1 to 80.8%.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the experimental data.

claims.claim: For 10 s decision windows, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test showed a significant difference between the linear model and the CNN (W = 16, p = 0.0203).
claims.source: Similarly, for 10 s decision windows, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test showed a significant difference between the two models (W = 16, p = 0.0203), with the CNN achieving a median accuracy of 85.1% compared to 75.7% for the linear model.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical test result based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: For 10 s decision windows, the CNN achieved a median accuracy of 85.1% compared to 75.7% for the linear model.
claims.source: Similarly, for 10 s decision windows, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test showed a significant difference between the two models (W = 16, p = 0.0203), with the CNN achieving a median accuracy of 85.1% compared to 75.7% for the linear model.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the experimental data.

claims.claim: The linear model achieves a median MESD of 22.6 s.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3, the linear model achieves a median MESD of 22.6 s, while the CNN achieves a median MESD of only 0.819 s.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The CNN achieves a median MESD of only 0.819 s.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3, the linear model achieves a median MESD of 22.6 s, while the CNN achieves a median MESD of only 0.819 s.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: A Wilcoxon signed-rank test shows the difference in MESD between the linear model and the CNN to be significant (W = 105, p < 0.001).
claims.source: A Wilcoxon signed-rank test shows this difference to be significant (W = 105, p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical test result based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: The extremely low MESD for the CNN is the result of the median accuracy still being 68.7% at only 0.13 s.
claims.source: The extremely low MESD for the CNN is the result of the median accuracy still being 68.7% at only 0.13 s, and the fact that the MESD typically chooses the optimal operation point at short decision window lengths (Geirnaert et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the MESD results with a citation.

claims.claim: The MESD typically chooses the optimal operation point at short decision window lengths.
claims.source: The extremely low MESD for the CNN is the result of the median accuracy still being 68.7% at only 0.13 s, and the fact that the MESD typically chooses the optimal operation point at short decision window lengths (Geirnaert et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Geirnaert et al., 2020.

claims.claim: For the two subjects with below 50% accuracy, the CNN performed poorly on story 1 and 2, but performed well on stories 3 and 4 (80% and higher).
claims.source: Our analysis shows that the results depend heavily on the story that is being tested on: for the two subjects with below 50% accuracy, the CNN performed poorly on story 1 and 2, but performed well on stories 3 and 4 (80% and higher).
claims.evidence: This is an analysis of the experimental data.

claims.claim: A linear mixed-effects model fit for decoding accuracy shows a significant effect of window length for the CNN model (df = 96, p < 0.001).
claims.source: A linear mixed-effects model fit for decoding accuracy, with decision window length as fixed effect and subject as random effect, shows a significant effect of window length for both the CNN model (df = 96, p < 0.001) and the linear model (df = 94, p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical test result based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: A linear mixed-effects model fit for decoding accuracy shows a significant effect of window length for the linear model (df = 94, p < 0.001).
claims.source: A linear mixed-effects model fit for decoding accuracy, with decision window length as fixed effect and subject as random effect, shows a significant effect of window length for both the CNN model (df = 96, p < 0.001) and the linear model (df = 94, p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical test result based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: The CNN uses mainly information from the beta band.
claims.source: Figure 5 shows that the CNN uses mainly information from the beta band, in line with Gao et al., 2017.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the results shown in Figure 5 and a citation.

claims.claim: The CNN shows primarily activations in the frontal and temporal regions, and to a lesser extent also in the occipital lobe.
claims.source: We see primarily activations in the frontal and temporal regions, and to a lesser extent also in the occipital lobe.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the analysis shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Activations in the CNN appear to be slightly stronger on the right side.
claims.source: Activations appear to be slightly stronger on the right side, as well.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the analysis shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: This result is in line with Ciccarelli et al., 2019, who also saw stronger activations in the frontal channels.
claims.source: This result is in line with Ciccarelli et al., 2019, who also saw stronger activations in the frontal channels (mostly for the 'Wet 18 CH' and 'Dry 18 CH' systems).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ciccarelli et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Gao et al., 2017 also found the frontal channels to significantly differ from the other channels within the beta band.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gao et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Using data from all trials, in addition to applying a per-trial MWF filter, results in a median decoding accuracy of 92.8% for decision windows of 1 s.

claims.evidence: This is a statistical test result based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: There is no statistically significant difference in decoding accuracy between leaving out both story and speaker and when using data of all trials without applying any spatial filtering for artifact removal (W = 48, p = 0.8077).
claims.source: There is, however, no statistically significant difference in decoding accuracy between leaving out both story and speaker and when using data of all trials, but without applying any spatial filtering for artifact removal (W = 48, p = 0.8077).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical test result based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: Having the same speaker and story in both the training and test set is less problematic than anticipated, provided they are preprocessed in a trial-independent way.

claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: For windows of 1 s, leaving out the test subject results in a significant decrease in decoding accuracy from 80.8% to 69.3% (W = 14, p = 0.0134).

claims.evidence: This is a statistical test result based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: For one subject, the network performs better when its data was not included during training.
claims.source: Surprisingly, for one subject the network performs better when its data was not included during training.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: The CNN model resulted in a significant increase in decoding accuracy compared to the linear model for decision windows as low as 1 s, with the CNN's median performance around 81%.
claims.source: The CNN model resulted in a significant increase in decoding accuracy compared to the linear model: for decision windows as low as 1 s, the CNN's median performance is around 81%.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results.

results.result: The study collected EEG data from 16 normal-hearing subjects using a 64-channel BioSemi ActiveTwo system at 8196 Hz while they listened to two competing speakers (four Dutch stories narrated by three male Flemish speakers) and were instructed to attend to one particular speaker. The experiment consisted of eight 6-minute trials with dichotic or HRTF-filtered presentation.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C38 provide a comprehensive description of the experimental setup, including subject population, recording equipment, stimulus characteristics, and trial structure. These methodological details are clearly stated and internally consistent, providing adequate documentation of the data collection procedure.

results.result: EEG data was preprocessed using bandpass filtering (1-9 Hz for linear models, 1-32 Hz for CNN), downsampling (20 Hz for linear, 128 Hz for CNN), MWF-based artifact removal, and subject-specific normalization. Data was divided into training, validation, and test sets using sliding windows with 50% overlap.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C46 describe the preprocessing pipeline with appropriate citations for key methodological choices (C40, C41, C43). The different preprocessing parameters for CNN vs. linear models are justified by prior work. The methodology is sufficiently detailed for replication.

results.result: The proposed CNN architecture consists of a convolutional layer with five 64×17 spatio-temporal filters (130 ms width), ReLu activation, average pooling over time, two fully connected layers (5 neurons with sigmoid, then 2 output neurons), and cross-entropy loss. The network has approximately 5500 parameters and was implemented in MATLAB 2016b with MatConvNet.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C57 provide a complete architectural description of the CNN model. The filter width optimization (C49) is based on validation set performance. The architecture is relatively simple and appropriate for the dataset size, though the justification for specific design choices (e.g., 5 filters, specific layer sizes) is limited.

results.result: The CNN was trained using a subject-specific approach with data from all subjects (including test subject but different trials) as regularization. A leave-one-story+speaker-out cross-validation scheme was used, retaining only two folds where speakers never appeared in both training and test sets. Training used mini-batch SGD with learning rate 0.09, momentum 0.9, step decay schedule, batch size 20, and weight decay regularization for 100 epochs.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C70 describe a rigorous training methodology with appropriate cross-validation to prevent overfitting to specific stories or speakers (C60-C62). Hyperparameters were determined by grid search (C70). The approach is well-justified, though the limitation to only 2 folds (C61) reduces the amount of usable data and may impact generalizability.

results.result: A linear stimulus reconstruction baseline model was implemented using spatio-temporal filtering with 250 ms delay, least-squares regression, and powerlaw subbands envelope extraction. The linear model was trained only on subject-specific data (unlike the CNN) and could not be evaluated at 0.13 s windows due to its 0.25 s kernel width.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C77, C80 describe the baseline model with appropriate citations (C72, C74). The different training approaches (C76) and fundamental differences between models (C77) are acknowledged. However, C77's claim that comparison should be treated with care is important—the models use different preprocessing and have fundamentally different capabilities, limiting direct comparability.

results.result: At 1 s decision windows, the CNN achieved significantly higher median accuracy (80.8%) compared to the linear model (58.1%) with W=3, p<0.001. At 10 s windows, the CNN achieved 85.1% vs. 75.7% for linear (W=16, p=0.0203). The CNN showed higher median accuracy but larger intersubject variability at both window lengths.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C86 report the primary performance comparison with appropriate statistical tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank). The results are supported by Figure 2. However, two subjects were excluded for <50% accuracy (C82), which may bias results positively. The increased intersubject variability (C81) is concerning and inadequately explained.

results.result: The CNN achieved a median MESD of 0.819 s compared to 22.6 s for the linear model (W=105, p<0.001). This extremely low MESD results from the CNN maintaining 68.7% median accuracy at 0.13 s windows, and the MESD metric typically selecting optimal operation points at short decision windows.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C91 report MESD results with appropriate statistics and cite the metric's definition (C91). The dramatic improvement is supported by Figure 3. However, C90 notes a caveat that the MESD metric assumes independent decisions, which may not hold for very short windows (<1 s), potentially underestimating actual switch time.

results.result: Window length significantly affects decoding accuracy for both models (CNN: df=96, p<0.001; Linear: df=94, p<0.001). However, the CNN shows much less degradation with shorter windows: from 10s to 1s, CNN accuracy decreases only 4.3% (85.1% to 80.8%) while linear decreases 17.6% (75.7% to 58.1%). At 0.25s, CNN achieves 74.0% vs. 53.4% for linear.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94, C111-C113 demonstrate a key advantage of the CNN using appropriate mixed-effects modeling and are supported by Figure 4. The CNN's robustness to short windows is a major finding. However, the explanation (C114-C115) for why this occurs is speculative and not directly tested.

results.result: Analysis of CNN filter weights shows the network primarily uses information from the beta frequency band, with activations concentrated in frontal and temporal regions (slightly stronger on the right side). These findings align with prior work showing beta band involvement in selective attention and frontal channel importance.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C99 provide interpretability analysis supported by Figures 5-6 and citations to consistent prior work (C95, C98, C99). However, the interpretation is limited: the authors acknowledge that backward decoder coefficients don't necessarily indicate neural response strength (text after C99), and they cannot exclude non-brain sources like eye movements (C117).

results.result: Using data from all trials with per-trial MWF filtering yields 92.8% accuracy vs. 80.8% for leave-one-story+speaker-out (W=91, p=0.0134), but without MWF there's no significant difference (W=48, p=0.8077). This demonstrates that per-trial data-driven preprocessing creates trial-specific fingerprints that enable overfitting, requiring trial-independent preprocessing for valid results.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C103, C118-C120 reveal an important methodological finding about preprocessing-induced overfitting, supported by Figure 7. The statistical tests are appropriate. This is a valuable contribution showing that common preprocessing approaches can invalidate results with spatio-temporal decoders. The recommendation (C119-C120) is well-justified by the data.

results.result: Subject-independent decoding (leave-one-subject-out) results in significantly decreased accuracy from 80.8% to 69.3% at 1s windows (W=14, p=0.0134). Surprisingly, one subject performed better when excluded from training.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C105 demonstrate that subject-specific training provides significant benefit, supported by Figure 8 and appropriate statistics. The anomalous subject (C105) is interesting but unexplained. The 11.5% accuracy decrease suggests subject-specific features are important, though 69.3% median accuracy for subject-independent decoding is still reasonable.

results.result: Two subjects had <50% accuracy at 10s windows and were excluded from analysis. The CNN shows high intersubject variability, with poorly performing subjects doing better on stories 3-4 (which were excluded from testing). The CNN achieves MESD ≤5s for 11/16 subjects (8 subjects <1s), but one subject has MESD of 33.4s and two have infinite MESD, indicating intersubject variability remains a challenge.
results.evaluation: Claims C82, C92, C109-C110, C127-C128, C131-C133 honestly report substantial intersubject variability and failure cases. The exclusion of 2/16 subjects (C82) is concerning and may inflate reported performance. The story-dependent performance (C92, C110) suggests potential overfitting despite cross-validation efforts. This variability is a significant limitation for practical applications.

results.result: The CNN significantly outperforms both the linear baseline and prior entropy-based direction classification methods, achieving 81% median accuracy at 1s windows and an unprecedented MESD of 0.819s, enabling robust neuro-steered volume control with acceptable latency.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 summarize the main findings with comparison to prior work (C107 cites Lu et al., 2018). The results represent a substantial advance in detection speed. However, the comparison to Lu et al. 2018 may not be entirely fair as different datasets and methods were used, and the high intersubject variability (C109, C133) tempers enthusiasm.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that the CNN's superior performance at short windows is because it directly decodes attention locus without relating neural activity to speech envelopes, avoiding the need for long-window correlation computations. Potential information sources include spatial brain activity patterns, but also possibly eye gaze or muscle activity reflected in EEG, which cannot be excluded.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C117 provide speculative explanations for the CNN's performance that are not directly tested. The hypothesis about why the CNN performs better (C114-C115) is plausible but unverified. Critically, C117 acknowledges that non-brain sources cannot be excluded despite control experiments, which is a major limitation in interpreting what the CNN actually decodes.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that observed variability is due to small dataset size and that the network needs more examples to generalize better. With more data, more complex CNN architectures would become feasible. Future improvements could include soft probabilistic decisions and LSTM extensions.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C125 are speculative suggestions for future work without supporting evidence. While plausible, the small dataset hypothesis (C121-C122) is not tested. The suggestions for architectural improvements (C123-C125) are reasonable but speculative. These represent future directions rather than supported findings.

results.result: For practical hearing aid applications, the CNN could steer beamformers toward attention direction without requiring clean speech envelopes. However, multiple issues require investigation including hearing loss effects, acoustic circumstances, attention switching mechanisms, computational complexity reduction, CNN pruning, and electrode reduction.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C139 discuss potential applications and required future work with appropriate citations (C136, C138, C139). However, these are speculative regarding practical implementation. The suggestion that the CNN could work without clean envelopes (C134) is promising but untested in realistic noisy conditions. The list of required investigations (C136-C139) is comprehensive but highlights how far the work is from practical deployment.

results.result: Beyond hearing aid applications, fast and accurate attention detection could enable measurement of subject compliance with attention instructions and allow tracking attention in almost real-time for studying attention dynamics and its interplay with eye gaze, speech intelligibility, and cognition.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C142 speculate about research applications without supporting evidence. While the fast detection speed could enable these applications, they are not demonstrated in this work. The suggestions are reasonable but represent potential future uses rather than validated capabilities.

results.result: The introduction establishes that humans can selectively attend to one speaker in multi-speaker scenarios (cocktail party problem), that EEG can decode attended speaker, but that short-window classification remains challenging. Prior work shows CNNs are effective for EEG classification and that attention direction is neurally encoded, particularly in alpha and beta bands.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C27 provide background context with appropriate citations throughout. These establish the scientific foundation and motivation for the study. The claims about prior work are properly attributed and the challenge of short-window decoding (C3, C20-C21) is well-documented. Some claims are speculative (C13, C25) but appropriately qualified.
